editorial:
The Paleface is a 21-minute two-reel silent comedy released January 1922 by First National Pictures, produced by Joseph M. Schenck and directed by Buster Keaton and Edward F. Cline. Keaton plays a hapless butterfly collector who stumbles into a standoff between a Native American tribe and a gang of oil-land swindlers; the tribe condemns him to death, he fashions asbestos underwear to survive a burning-at-the-stake, and is adopted as 'Little Chief Paleface' before helping recover the tribe's stolen land deed. First National never renewed the copyright in 1949â€“1950, and no renewal entry appears in either year's CCE Part 14A records â€” the film has been circulating freely for decades and is a dependable mid-length short for compilations, silent-comedy retrospectives, and illustrative documentary clips.

The one practical trap is the restoration layer. Kino Lorber holds a 2K restoration in its Shorts Collection 1917â€“1923 Blu-ray, and Cohen Film Collection holds a separate restoration by Cineteca di Bologna at L'Immagine Ritrovata Laboratory â€” both are independently copyrighted derivative works. Archive.org hosts earlier unrestored transfers; use those, not the polished restoration releases. Any musical score found on a copy is also separately protected: the 1922 film was released silent, so no score is covered by the public-domain print.
faq: Can I use footage from The Paleface (1922) in a documentary or online video?

Yes â€” the underlying silent print is public domain. First National Pictures did not file a copyright renewal in 1949â€“1950, so protection lapsed at the end of the 28-year initial term. Source your footage from an unrestored archive.org transfer rather than from the Kino Lorber or Cohen Film Collection restoration releases, which carry their own modern copyright.
Does the film come with usable music?

No. The 1922 release was silent with no synchronized score; nothing on the audio side is covered by the film's public-domain status. Any music you find on a particular copy â€” a restoration track, a user-composed accompaniment â€” is a separately copyrighted work. You must license music independently or compose your own.
